item.title: Portland Trail Blazers fire new play-by-play broadcaster hours after hiring announced
item.dc:creator: KPTV News staff, Jordan Gartner
item.description: The Portland Trail Blazers have fired newly hired play-by-play broadcaster Braiden Bell.
item.content:encoded:
PORTLAND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - The Portland Trail Blazers have fired newly hired play-by-play broadcaster Braiden Bell.

According to a statement from the team, Bell’s termination stemmed from social media posts that violated team and league policies about racist, sexist and harmful comments.

“The Portland Trail Blazers have zero tolerance for racist, sexist or harmful comments,” the team said with the announcement. “The play-by-play role carries a long legacy of excellence ... and we hold that standard without exception.”

Bell had been announced as the team’s new play-by-play announcer just hours before his firing.

“We did not meet our own bar in this process, and for that we apologize to Blazers fans and Rip City,” the team continued. “We will make sure that our new broadcaster reflects our values.”

Bell graduated from Arizona State University, where he called games for the basketball team.

Before his brief stint with the Trail Blazers, Bell also called games for California Baptist University, as well as being the play-by-play announcer for the Phoenix Mercury and working games in the NBA G League.

Bell said he was “deeply sorry” for the language that he used in previous posts on social media following his dismissal from the team.

“Those tweets, while wrong, were written by me 14 years ago while I was only 15 years old and have no reflection of who I am today. I do not take lightly any harm it causes now,” Bell’s message read. “I’d like to apologize to anyone who was hurt by my words and will continue to always treat people with kindness and respect.”

The 2026-27 NBA regular season begins on Oct. 20, with the Trail Blazers’ first preseason game scheduled for Oct. 7.

media:content.media:description: Bell, an Arizona State University graduate, served as the play-by-play announcer for Sun Devil Athletics and the Valley Suns in 2024 before joining the Mercury in 2025.

item.title: 911 call reveals concerns about well-being of 2 children found dead from starvation at home
item.dc:creator: Marissa Thompson, Elijah Brown, Jordan Gartner
item.description: Two children who were found dead in a home earlier this week in South Carolina have been identified.
item.content:encoded:
LADSON, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — Two children who were found dead in a home earlier this week in South Carolina have been identified, and authorities said this wasn’t the first time they had been called to the residence.

Emory Deacon, 2, and Harlow Deacon, 15 months old, died of starvation and dehydration due to neglect, Charleston County coroner Bobbi Jo O’Neal said.

Justine May, the children’s mother and described as their primary caregiver, has been charged in the case with two counts of homicide by child abuse.

According to the Charleston County Sheriff’s Office, deputies had responded to numerous calls at the Pinewood Drive residence before ultimately finding the two children dead during a welfare check at the home.

The previous calls to the home were said to have included welfare checks and visits coordinated with the South Carolina Department of Social Services and the South Carolina Department of Mental Health Mobile Crisis Unit.

Authorities said deputies made contact with May and the children in August and again several more times in September, noting they observed no signs of concern during those visits.

On Tuesday, authorities said they were called back to the home after a 911 call came through that morning asking deputies to conduct a welfare check on the two young girls after they had not been seen, with their mother acting differently while walking around the neighborhood by herself.

“I’m just concerned because she didn’t have her kids, and nobody has seen her kids,” the caller told the Charleston County 911 dispatcher. “She was walking down the road today, and she didn’t have her babies, and that’s not like her.”

When deputies arrived at the home that afternoon, they said May exited the house and was crying and speaking incoherently. Upon entering, that’s when they saw the two children dead.

May was taken into custody.

According to affidavits, after being read her Miranda rights, May told detectives that she had spent the previous two weeks in a “blur,” saying she could not remember the last time she fed Emory and Harlow or gave them anything to drink.

Authorities said May told detectives that she believed her children were dead because they did not eat. She reportedly told deputies that she knew that not feeding her children was neglectful and confirmed she had been the only one present at home and was the sole caregiver for the girls over the last few weeks.

May remains jailed at the Al Cannon Detention Center.

item.title: Recycling facility helps police catch suspect after 77 fire hydrants damaged
item.dc:creator: Casey Zanowic, Gray News staff
item.description: Scrap yards are usually full of metal and hidden treasures, but this week, one of those yards helped police haul in something else - a scrap thief.
item.content:encoded:
ST. LOUIS (KMOV/Gray News) - Scrap yards are usually full of metal and hidden treasures, but this week, one of those yards helped police haul in something else - a scrap thief.

“Naturally, when they approached me, I was very happy to help and do anything I could and step forward and give them the information they needed,” Phillip Harbison, general manager at SA Recycling in St. Louis, exclaimed.

The recycling facility, located off of the Broadway, helped find the man who put countless lives in jeopardy.

“I genuinely just dislike thieves; I’m not a fan of thieves at all,” Harbison stated. “So it’s very important to me to get them off the street, and especially when they’re doing things that can harm our community.”

Over the past week, police have been searching for a suspect accused of damaging and stealing the components off of 77 fire hydrants across the City of St. Louis.

On Thursday, police arrested 65-year-old Harry Farmer in connection with that vandalism after they said surveillance video caught him sawing off the hydrants’ brass valves.

“We had a citizen who came forward. We were able to get video of this individual. We were able to obtain a name, but we had to do a case to make sure that we got it right, got the evidence, and then we had to track down video at each one of these known locations,” Chief Robert Tracy, St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department, said.

Farmer allegedly went to SA Recycling to sell the valves, which is when Harbison got him on camera and a picture of his ID.

“All the way from the second they pull onto this lot, they’re on camera,” he explained. “We have pictures of their ID; everything is stored in our database, so every transaction will have a picture of the material they brought in, of their ID, license plate, all of that.”

When police came to ask if they had any information about these incidents, Harbison said they were happy to cooperate.

“You don’t want those types of people out in the city and I want to stop the bad name that’s being given to scrap yards, and that’s why we keep the records we do and are able to help when the police do come and ask for help,” he stated.

Farmer has now been charged with eight felonies.

“Damaging fire hydrants creates a major public safety risk,” Chief Tracy said. “Firefighters depend on working hydrants to protect lives and property - interfering with that access puts residents, businesses and first responders in danger.”

“I’ve been Fire Chief for 19 years, been in this city for 48 with the fire department. I’ve never, ever seen anything like this. Traveled around the country, I’ve never seen hydrants vandalized like this intentionally,” Chief Dennis Jenkerson, St. Louis Fire Department, stated.

For recycling facilities like Harbisons, they just have one message to other scrap thieves.

“I will not buy it; don’t bring it to SA Recycling. SA Recycling does not want stolen scrap… some of us will absolutely do our part and help the community and put criminals behind bars," he said.

As of Friday evening, Farmer is in custody, but police still have to extradite him back to Missouri from Illinois.

The investigation remains ongoing. Police want anyone with more information on the damaged hydrants to contact 314-444-2500 and talk to District 4 detectives.

media:content.media:description: Local recycling facility helps police catch suspect after 77 St. Louis fire hydrants were damaged

item.title: Bicyclist dies after being struck by vehicle near Keehi Marina
item.dc:creator: HNN Staff
item.description: As a result, the bicyclist was ejected onto the roadway and was pronounced dead at the scene.
item.content:encoded:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - A bicyclist was killed Friday morning after being struck by a vehicle on Sand Island Access Road near Keehi Marina.

The incident happened at 7:10 a.m.

The Honolulu Police Department said a 34-year-old man was driving eastbound on Sand Island Access Road near Keehi Marina Boat Harbor when he struck a bicyclist, an unidentified man, who was traveling on Sand Island Access in the same direction.

As a result, the bicyclist was ejected onto the roadway and was pronounced dead at the scene. Police said the bicyclist was not wearing a helmet.

The 34-year-old driver and his 34-year-old passenger were not injured as a result of the collision.

At this time, speed, drugs, or alcohol do not appear to be a contributing factor in this collision.

This is the 31st traffic fatality on Oahu this year, compared to 68 at the same time in 2025.

The investigation is ongoing.

media:content.media:description: The incident happened at 7:10 a.m.

item.title: Grand jury indicts 24-year-old woman in fatal Kailua Target shooting
item.dc:creator: HNN Staff
item.description: The charges stem from a Sept. 26 shooting in the parking lot of the Target store in Kailua.
item.content:encoded:
HONOLULU (HawaiiNewsNow) - A grand jury indicted Hilinaikailimakualopali Keeno, 24, for murder in the second degree in connection with the fatal shooting of 30-year-old Thomas Malone.

Keeno was also indicted on charges of carrying or using a firearm in the commission of a separate felony and a place to keep. Prosecutors also charged her as a multiple offender.

The charges stem from a Sept. 26 shooting in the parking lot of the Target store in Kailua.

Murder in the second degree carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment with the possibility of parole.

If a jury finds that the prosecution has met its burden for the imposition of extended terms of imprisonment, Keeno could face life imprisonment without the possibility of parole for murder in the second degree, life imprisonment for the class A felony, and up to 10 years for the class C felony.

Keeno is being held at the Oahu Community Corrections Center.

Keeno is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

item.title: Wife hid husband’s remains in freezer for 7 years to collect benefits, police say
item.dc:creator: Hannah Lee, Akim Powell
item.description: A woman in Alaska hid her late husband’s remains in a freezer for years in order to collect benefits, according to authorities.
item.content:encoded:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska. (KTUU/Gray News) - A woman in Alaska hid her late husband’s remains in a freezer for years in order to collect benefits, according to authorities.

Juneau police found the remains of Ross Pasquan inside a chest freezer on July 19. Police said he would have been 74 years old at the time of the discovery of his remains.

A family member had been cleaning out the property following the death of Pasquan’s wife, Sheryl Ann McDonald-Pasquan, who died on July 14, 2025, from natural causes.

Inside a storage shed, a family member discovered a locked freezer.

Police said the person found the key, opened the freezer and found a tarp-wrapped object that appeared to contain human remains. They closed the freezer and went directly to Juneau police.

The State Medical Examiner’s Office determined that Pasquan died of natural causes related to severe cardiovascular disease. Investigators believe Pasquan’s remains were placed in the freezer sometime between 2018 and 2025.

The investigation found that McDonald-Pasquan concealed his death and continued applying for and receiving benefits in his name until her death. Those benefits included Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend checks, Social Security benefits and retirement benefits.

Investigators also learned that a retirement benefit provider had not been notified of his death and was still depositing monthly payments into Pasquan’s account up until July 2026.

Investigators found no evidence that another person caused Pasquan’s death or helped McDonald-Pasquan in concealing his remains or collecting his benefits.

Witness interviews indicated that Pasquan had a history of significant health problems and that McDonald-Pasquan served as his primary caregiver. Witnesses said she explained his absence by telling them he had been moved to a care facility outside Juneau.

The investigation is now closed due to McDonald-Pasquan’s death.

media:content.media:description: Ross Pasquan was found deceased in a freezer on July 19th, 2026.

item.title: Group of Seven to release barrels of stockpiled fuel
item.dc:creator: Caitrin Assaf
item.description: Amid record global diesel prices, a group of some of the world’s largest economies will release millions of barrels of stockpiled fuel in an effort to cap the soaring cost.
item.content:encoded:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The Group of Seven - a collection of some of the world’s largest economies - announced on Friday the release of 100 million barrels of fuel from its emergency stockpile following record-high fuel prices in September.

Oil prices have risen to record levels globally. The G7’s release of crude and diesel barrels marks a rare move intended to cap the cost of diesel.

The barrels come from the G7’s emergency stockpile, which is set aside for global supply shortages.

Wars in Ukraine and Iran have reduced the global fuel supply. Diesel has been particularly affected, with American farmers and the shipping industry facing a heavy impact.

With the midterm elections now days away, the Trump administration had considered restricting U.S. diesel exports, including a possible outright ban, to lower costs before November.

The G7’s release appears to end that possibility; the group’s statement said the release comes with an agreement among member nations not to limit energy exports to allied countries.

President Trump said in a Truth Social post the process will begin “immediately.” French President Emmanuel Macron said the release would happen over four months.

The move could reduce diesel prices by a few cents per gallon, according to experts, who added the effect would likely be temporary. Releasing stockpiled barrels does little to increase refinery capacity or production, experts said.

item.title: Catering business shut down after football team suffers food poisoning before game
item.dc:creator: Jayla Louis, Jordan Gartner
item.description: An unlicensed home-based catering business in Illinois has been ordered to cease operations after dozens of people were sickened.
item.content:encoded:
ROCK ISLAND, Ill. (KWQC/Gray News) - An unlicensed home-based catering business in Illinois has been ordered to cease operations after dozens of people were sickened at a football team dinner.

According to the Rock Island Health Department, it was notified of a foodborne illness outbreak that stemmed from a Rock Island football team dinner that took place on Sept. 24 in the school cafeteria.

Health department officials said the dinner was catered by a home-based business called Sunshine and Spice.

Players, coaches and parents who attended the dinner were served fajita chicken, seasoned taco beef, cheese, flour taco shells, cheesy pepper beans, cilantro corn rice and Pico de Gallo salsa.

Seventy-five people were served the meal, and at least 45 were reported sick, causing the team to postpone its homecoming football game.

Just hours after the dinner, 23 players, five coaches and three parents reported symptoms, which included vomiting and diarrhea.

Officials said no one was hospitalized, but one player did have to visit a doctor.

The health department reported that most symptoms were over within 24 hours.

Health department officials noted that they met with the owner of Sunshine and Spice and learned the business was unlicensed and not food-safety certified. They then ordered the business to shut down, with the option of getting properly certified.

Officials said the owner told the health department that all ingredients were purchased from the Moline Walmart, Spotted Apron in Geneseo and farmers’ markets in Davenport and Coal Valley.

Joshua Harris, owner of Sunshine and Spice, released the following statement regarding the situation:

“First, Sunshine and Spice wants to sincerely apologize and send even more prayers to anyone affected by last week’s Rock Island football team meal.

We provided a taco bar-style potluck before the team was dismissed to prepare for their homecoming game. All of the food purchased from Walmart was fully cooked. We put all of the leftovers in plastic bags provided by the team parents for anyone to take home.

We have cooked for numerous parents of the team/school in the past and have no reason ever to provide a sub-standard meal or purposely attempt any tampering shenanigans. We are saddened by this whole situation.

We have been working side by side with the Rock Island County Health Department and Rock Island City/County Law Enforcement Agencies to be a part of their continuing investigations.

Again, we want to extend our deepest apologies and continued prayers to those affected.”

The investigation into the food poisoning remained active pending test results for pathogens in the food seized by the county, health officials said.

item.title: ‘A psychopath’: Professional boxer arrested after 2-year-old dies, 1-year-old hurt in alleged abuse
item.dc:creator: David Baker, Micaela Marshall, Jordan Gartner
item.description: A professional boxer is facing a first-degree murder charge after police say he beat and killed his girlfriend’s 2-year-old son and abused his own 1-year-old child.
item.content:encoded:
MESA, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — A professional boxer is facing a first-degree murder charge after police say he beat and killed his girlfriend’s 2-year-old son and abused his own 1-year-old child.

Mesa police said the situation started Tuesday when paramedics responded to an apartment for a child in medical distress. First responders rushed the toddler to a hospital, where he died from his injuries.

Doctors noted suspicious bruising was found across the child’s body and contacted police, triggering a homicide investigation.

Investigators identified Kishawn Porter, 23, a professional fighter, as the suspect in the case.

Authorities said that while Porter is a professional fighter, bruising found across his knuckles did not come from training or competition, but rather from fatal child abuse.

Porter was taken into police custody on Tuesday.

“Mr. Porter hit and punched the 2-year-old victim multiple times with either his hands and/or a sandal,” a prosecutor with the Maricopa County Attorney’s Office said during Porter’s initial court appearance.

During Porter’s court appearance, prosecutors outlined a violent juvenile history, telling the judge Porter has prior adjudications for child molestation and aggravated assault involving a restrained victim.

An autopsy conducted Wednesday by the Maricopa County medical examiner revealed catastrophic internal trauma on the child that included healing and acute rib fractures, a lacerated liver and a lacerated stomach, with blood found pooling in the abdomen.

“It takes a substantial amount of force to lacerate the stomach, and the injuries were all consistent with child abuse,” court records stated. “Based on the injuries, no one could have survived the severity.”

Forensic experts noted that the child’s healing rib fractures pointed to a pattern of ongoing violence in the home rather than an isolated incident.

“That means this wasn’t the only attack,” Dr. Roy Lubit, a forensic psychiatrist who specializes in child abuse cases, said. “The idea of beating and killing an infant indicates an almost basic lack of humanity. An individual who would do the acts that are alleged would almost be overwhelmingly likely to be a psychopath.”

Detectives said Porter also abused his own 1-year-old child by spanking him, hitting him in the mouth and slapping his torso and rib cage.

Formal charges regarding the allegations involving the 1-year-old have not yet been submitted to prosecutors.

Following his arrest, two combat sports promotions announced they had cut ties with Porter due to the severity of the charges.

A judge set Porter’s bond at $1.5 million.

media:content.media:description: Kishawn Porter, 23, was arrested Tuesday.

item.title: InvestigateTV+ Weekend: Sacrificing Safety?
item.dc:creator: Brandon Wissbaum
item.description: A crash can change a life in seconds and in many American cars, a safety feature designed to keep front-seat passengers from hitting each other is still missing.
item.content:encoded:
(InvestigateTV) — A crash can change a life in seconds and in many American cars, a safety feature designed to keep front-seat passengers from hitting each other is still missing.

Plus, when deadly crashes keep happening, families want more than promises — they want safer streets before another life is lost.

Sacrificing Safety?

They’re an auto safety innovation in cars around the world: airbags that can protect you and your front-seat passenger from hitting each other in a side-impact crash. When drivers and front-seat passengers collide, the result can be serious head injuries or death. But even though those airbags were first introduced in the U.S., many cars here don’t have them. Why?

Crash tests in Europe in 2020 drove the adoption of those airbags, but the U.S. doesn’t do that type of testing. Authorities here question whether the airbags are necessary – but the world’s largest auto safety equipment supplier tells us lives are being lost unnecessarily due to the lack of airbags that manufacturers already know how to incorporate into their vehicles.

We’ll speak with one accident victim who says a front-center airbag could have prevented her from suffering a devastating head injury and the lifelong consequences.

Read more

A goal to end traffic deaths by 2050. Is it working?

More than 36,000 people were killed on American roads last year — according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration — a reminder that for too many families, a routine drive can end in tragedy.

In Phoenix, city leaders are trying to reduce deadly crashes — but acknowledge the work is far from done. Reporter Amy Cutler looks at the city’s safety plan, the gaps that remain, and one family’s loss.

Read more

Loud car modifications: What’s legal, what’s not

For many people, a quiet night at home or a meal outside can be interrupted in an instant by the roar of a revving engine or a backfiring exhaust.

In North Carolina — as in many states — vehicles must meet muffler and exhaust requirements. But police say catching violators can be difficult. Reporter Jamie Boll in Charlotte explains what’s legal, what isn’t, and why neighbors want action.

Read more

How ‘convenient spending’ could drain your budget

We all do it from time to time – shell out money to save a little time or make life easier. It’s called convenient spending.

In this Watching Your Wallet, Consumer Investigator Rachel DePompa shows us why convenience can act like a monthly trap, silently draining your budget.

Read more

item.title: Trump to stump for Husted, Ramaswamy in Ohio
item.dc:creator: Molly Martinez
item.description: President Donald Trump will travel to Vandalia, Ohio, Saturday to campaign for Republican Sen. Jon Husted and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy.
item.content:encoded:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump will travel to Vandalia, Ohio, Saturday to campaign for Republican Sen. Jon Husted and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy.

The visit comes as new polling shows Democrat Sherrod Brown leading Husted by 8 points, according to Marist.

Ohio has voted reliably Republican in recent elections, and Trump won the state three times. But 56% of Ohio voters strongly disapprove of the job Trump is doing, according to the report.

Swing-state candidates face a decision on whether to align with Trump or distance themselves from the administration’s policies, according to the report.

The Saturday stop is part of a 32-day series of rallies that also includes Iowa, Florida, Alaska and Nebraska.

item.title: Mother accused of letting 7-year-old daughter’s teeth decay, leaving her unable to eat solid food
item.dc:creator: Akim Powell
item.description: A mother in Pennsylvania is accused of allowing her 7-year-old daughter’s teeth to decay so badly that the girl could not eat solid food or live without pain.
item.content:encoded:
(Gray News) - A mother in Pennsylvania is accused of allowing her 7-year-old daughter’s teeth to decay so badly that the girl could not eat solid food or live without pain.

Maria Lopez-Paz, 39, was charged with endangering the welfare of a child.

On Sept. 10, Scranton police responded to reports of a child not being fed, as well as possible drug use in the home, according to the Scranton Times Tribune.

Officers spoke with a county Office of Youth and Family Services case manager, who reported the child was not attending school because she was not vaccinated.

Police scheduled an emergency interview and medical assessment with the child.

During the interview, the 7-year-old told officers the only time she was without pain was when she was asleep. She also raised concerns about cockroaches, rats and bugs in the home, according to the complaint.

The child said when she was hungry, she drank milk.

On Sept. 14, caseworkers took the girl to the dentist, where staff determined the girl had never had any dental care.

The girl suffered from 10 cavities and large areas of decay and needed multiple extractions and procedures.

Investigators also noted the juvenile had not seen a doctor since 2024, when the family moved to Pennsylvania.

A preliminary hearing is scheduled for 11 a.m. Oct. 14 before District Judge Laura Turlip.

item.title: Coming out later in life: Why more LGBTQ+ older adults are living openly
item.dc:creator: LeAnne Gendreau, Katherine Ambrose , Sondra 'Sam' Cradduck , Amy Amy Cameron O’Rourke, Rhea Rogers
item.description: We explore the courage, newfound freedom and unique challenges of coming out later in life.
item.content:encoded:
(Aging Untold) — Aging brings changes beyond the physical — it can reshape courage, confidence and a sense of self. For some older adults in the LGBTQ+ community, that growth shows up as coming out later in life after decades of keeping part of who they are hidden.

The Aging Untold experts are exploring what shifts with age that make living openly feel possible, and what’s still at stake for couples who choose to stay private.

What finally makes it feel safe to come out

Katherine Ambrose, an aging-well coach, opened the conversation by asking what changes as people get older that can make them feel safe enough to live more openly.

“I think the thing that changes the most is judgmental people pass away,” Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “I think if you’re trying to keep it from your own parents, and once they’re gone, you’re able to be who you are.”

Cradduck said the shift can also come from a child who wasn’t able to accept it, and later changes their mind — sometimes because someone else in their life has come out.

“It gives you an opportunity, plus the fear of your own mortality and not being able to end your life with the person you want to end your life with and having them beside you,” Cradduck said. “That can be very overwhelming. So you finally throw caution to the wind, and you no longer care what other people think. You care who’s beside you during those final moments. So you let the world know. And I see nothing wrong with that.”

A 50-year relationship kept secret

Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared a story from her own work: two women in their early 80s went into her office for help, and she could feel the love between them.

“I said, how long have you two been together? And they said, 50 years,” O’Rourke said. “Not married. And I said, ‘Does anybody in your family know?’ And they said, ‘No.’”

When O’Rourke asked the women what had stopped them from telling their families, they said they were too scared.

“They’re not going to accept it. We just kept everything the way it is,” they told O’Rourke.

“I felt sad. I would want them to have more, but I could tell that they had forged such a close bond that the decision worked for them,” O’Rourke said.

O’Rourke said her advice for couples in that position is to be direct with family ahead of time.

“Let everybody know ahead of time, this is what we’re doing. This is who I am. This is what I want from you,” O’Rourke said. “These are the boundaries that I’m drawing for myself that I want you to abide by.”

Ambrose added that verbal wishes aren’t enough on their own.

“There’s some real nasty people when it comes to death and hospitals, etc., or who’s making decisions on the funerals,” Ambrose said. “It’s really important to have legal documents in place.”

When families shut partners out

Cradduck shared a story of a woman she provided care for.

The woman’s best friend was also her partner. During the woman’s final days in hospice care, her family forbade her partner from visiting — and wouldn’t let her attend the funeral to pay her respects, Cradduck saod.

“I’ve seen where families step in and they do the most horrific thing,” Cradduck said. “They’re protecting their own image of who this person was instead of accepting them.”

Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said there is a physical toll that comes with hiding one’s identity for years.

“Once you become older, a lot of times I think people just own who they are. They’re authentic,” Rogers said. “When you’re living unseen and unheard, that’s an emotional burden, that’s loneliness, that’s stress. And that’s a whole bunch of physiology affecting your body.”

Cradduck also noted a gap in elder care options for LGBTQ+ seniors.

“We haven’t built enough communities for our aged population at all, but we don’t have enough LGBTQ-friendly companies and care companies,” Cradduck said.

She pointed to SAGE USA, which she described as an LGBTQ-friendly training program that helps communities, assisted living facilities and home care agencies work with elderly people in the community.

Coming out — or staying private — is a personal choice

O’Rourke said the decision to come out later in life comes with its own mix of emotions.

“You’re going to have grief associated with losing some people that might not accept it. You’ll have your own grief of changing from one identity to another,” O’Rourke said. “But you can have two feelings at the same time. You can feel sad. You can also feel celebratory. You can feel happy that you’re finally yourself.”

Cradduck said staying private can be the right call for some.

“If staying in the closet is what’s safest and what’s best, and what brings the least amount of stress and turmoil — then live your life that way,” Cradduck said.

O’Rourke added that religious beliefs are worth acknowledging as part of that decision as well.

“I think that’s important to acknowledge, but I’m with you — do whatever you feel comfortable with,” O’Rourke said.

Rogers also emphasized protecting those choices legally.

“Do whatever you feel comfortable with, but take the legal actions to protect,” Rogers said.

Ambrose added that younger generations may not fully grasp what older LGBTQ+ adults faced.

“Younger generations underestimate the amount of fear, stigma, pressure that was on us decades ago,” Ambrose said. “Some of the more controversial things that didn’t fit in the box, it was a really hard thing to live in. And I just believe we’re living in a more empowering age, and hopefully learning to act with a little more love and kindness.”

item.title: The anti-bucket list: Why letting go might be a secret to aging well
item.dc:creator: LeAnne Gendreau, Katherine Ambrose , Sondra 'Sam' Cradduck , Amy Amy Cameron O’Rourke, Rhea Rogers
item.description: Creating an "anti-bucket list" can help you let go of guilt, grudges and obligations as you age.
item.content:encoded:
(Aging Untold) — A bucket list is about everything you still want to do. But what about an “anti-bucket list” — the things you’re finally ready to stop doing, stop caring about or stop apologizing for?

Saying no might be one of the most powerful tools for a freer, more joyful life after 60.

The problem with automatic “yes”

Aging expert Amy O’Rourke kicked off the conversation with a true confession.

“I was asked to be on the HOA (homeowners association) board, and I said yes immediately,” O’Rourke said. “And then I went home and I was like, what did I say yes for? I don’t want to do that.”

O’Rourke said she had agreed out of guilt rather than genuine desire.

“I said it out of guilt that I should, that I can, that I would — afraid of what other people would think,” O’Rourke said. “So I reneged, and immediately I had better energy. I had better clarity. I got through the discomfort of saying no when I’m used to saying yes to everything.”

Subtraction as a privilege of aging

Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose framed the shift as a kind of wisdom that comes with age.

“It’s a discernment. You hope as you get older, you become wiser and you make maybe more mature choices,” Ambrose said.

“One of the privileges of getting older is subtraction,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, added. “What can I do to subtract that’s going to give me more peace, more sleep, more joy. And it’s OK.”

Rogers said adding too many obligations creates stress that the body can’t distinguish from any other kind.

“Your body doesn’t realize the difference between types of stress, because it’s going to react the same,” Rogers said.

Gerontologist Sam Cradduck noted that saying yes isn’t always the wrong move.

“Sometimes yes is purpose,” Cradduck said. “Some people will say yes because it does give them the purpose, and we still need to feel that.”

Practicing the word “no”

Cradduck said the hardest habits to break are often the ones tied to people, boards and other obligations, like hosting Thanksgiving dinner year after year.

“I don’t want to fix Thanksgiving dinner anymore kind of thing,” Cradduck said, describing the kind of thought many people are afraid to say out loud. “I’ve done it for 35 years. Daughter, son, you can cook and it’s time for you to take it on.”

O’Rourke suggested starting small for anyone too anxious to say no to a big obligation right away.

“So maybe you start by saying something to someone other than a family member — say no and practice. Or if you’re really anxiety-ridden, say the words out loud to yourself. Kind of rehearse the conversation,” O’Rourke said.

Ambrose shared a story to illustrate the point, about a couple in their late 70s who had recently married.

“She was telling me about all the Thanksgivings and things that she’d hosted, what she could cook,” Ambrose said. “And he was so shocked. He said, ‘You told me you can’t cook.’ She said, ‘No, I didn’t say I can’t cook — I said I don’t cook.’”

“It can be very freeing,” Ambrose said. “I think as time becomes shorter, you start thinking about what I really want to do.”

Key takeaways

  1. An “anti-bucket list” is about subtraction, not addition.
  2. Guilt-driven “yes” answers can drain energy.
  3. The body reacts to different types of stress the same way.
  4. Not all “yes” answers are bad — some provide purpose.
  5. Practice saying no in low-stakes situations first.

media:content.media:description: Forget adding more to your plate — subtract as you get older with an anti-bucket list.

item.title: The breakup nobody talks about: Losing a friend as you age
item.dc:creator: LeAnne Gendreau, Katherine Ambrose , Sondra 'Sam' Cradduck , Amy Amy Cameron O’Rourke, Rhea Rogers
item.description: We are exploring how to make peace with shifting priorities and move forward without guilt when lifelong friendships begin to fade.
item.content:encoded:
(Aging Untold) — Some friendships are built over decades of shared memories, routines and common ground. But as politics shift, priorities change and people grow in different directions, even the closest bonds can quietly come apart.

“It’s not talked about a lot”

Losing a friend later in life can hit just as hard as any other breakup, but friendship loss is often grieved in silence, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said.

“I think people grieve over lost friendships, and they don’t talk about it because it seems bad or wrong or uncommon, or they discount it,” O’Rourke said.

During a dinner with friends, the conversation drifted toward politics, O’Rourke said.

“We all agreed that that was a topic we were not going to bring up because our friendship meant more than a topic,” O’Rourke said. “I love the maturity of the friendships that we acknowledged it so it could be sustained.”

Why losing a friend can feel like a broken heart

“I don’t think people realize that not every broken heart comes from romance,” Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said. “There are a lot of really deeply broken hearts from severed families and severed friendships. We don’t give enough credence to it, and we certainly don’t allow people to normally grieve it.”

When someone loses a spouse or goes through a divorce, people rally around them. That support often doesn’t show up the same way when a friendship ends.

“Nobody’s bringing you casseroles or sending you flowers usually, and it can be really tough,” aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said.

Don’t put all your friendship “eggs in one basket”

O’Rourke said she isn’t a fan of relying on a single best friend.

“I like the idea of having friendships broader — broader in age, broader in number — so that you’re enhanced in all areas of your life,” O’Rourke said. “And if one friendship changes, you’re not completely unraveled.”

Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, agreed, comparing close friendships to relationships that end the way marriages sometimes do.

“I see people as they grow as kind of like people who get divorced,” Rogers said. “They grow apart for whatever reason.”

When a friendship is one-sided

O’Rourke described watching a friendship where one person consistently gave and the other consistently took — until the giver stopped.

“The giver kind of woke up and thought, ‘I’m not going to give anymore,’” O’Rourke said. “And it ended. Those that were watching it thought, ‘Oh, a sigh of relief.’ But they both went through grief.”

Moving forward after a friendship ends

Ambrose shared how a recent friendship breakup affected her personally, including during a family vacation.

“I was so shocked to have this end that it devastated me, and it ruined a vacation that was very important to me with my husband and son,” Ambrose said.

Her advice: don’t let the loss take over.

“Don’t let people ruin your day, your vacation,” Ambrose said. “Just accept it for what it is. Embrace it and get over it. They’re doing things for their reasons, and it’s maybe none of your business. Stay out of judgment. Don’t try to figure them out — go on and just say next.”

Ambrose added that picking yourself back up opens the door to new connections.

“It can be really tough grief, but pick yourself up because you have the opportunity to find new joy, new happiness,” Ambrose said. “You never know when you’re going to meet your next friends. So give yourself that gift and get back out there.”

Key takeaways

  1. Friendship loss deserves real grief. Losing a close friend can be as painful as a romantic breakup, but it rarely comes with the same outside support.
  2. Talk about it before it breaks. Setting boundaries, like agreeing not to discuss divisive topics, can help sustain long-term friendships.
  3. Diversify your friendships. Having a broad circle of friends across different ages and backgrounds can soften the blow if one relationship ends.
  4. Watch for one-sided dynamics. Friendships where one person always gives and the other always takes often end — and both people grieve, even if outsiders feel relief.
  5. Don’t let the loss take over your life. Accept the friendship for what it was, resist the urge to over-analyze the other person’s reasons and keep moving forward.
  6. Stay open to new connections. New friendships can bring new joy, even after a painful loss.

media:content.media:description: When a friendship ends later in life, the grief is real.

item.title: Firefighters extinguish 2-alarm fire at Leeward Drive Inn restaurant in Waipahu
item.dc:creator: HNN Staff
item.description: Honolulu Fire Department crews were called out to the scene near Farrington Highway and Pupukahi Street just before 4:30 a.m. on Friday.
item.content:encoded:
WAIPAHU (HawaiiNewsNow) - Firefighters battled a 2-alarm building fire at Leeward Drive Inna, a landmark Korean restaurant in Waipahu early Friday morning.

Honolulu Fire Department crews were called out to the scene near Farrington Highway and Pupukahi Street just before 4:30 a.m. on Friday.

The first unit arrived at 4:35 a.m. and found smoke on all sides and flames through the roof.

Firefighters secured a water supply and initiated an aggressive offensive fire attack with an aerial ladder fire stream and handlines.

Overhaul techniques were performed on the rooftop and in the ceiling to extinguish smoldering materials while looking for hidden fires.

The fire was extinguished at 6:50 a.m., and the scene was cleared shortly after.

The restaurant will be closed Friday after the building sustained extensive interior damage.

No one was injured, and HFD said all searches confirmed no one was inside.

The HFD Fire Investigator was requested to determine the origin and cause of the fire and provide damage estimates.

Honolulu police and Emergency Medical Services were also on the scene.

media:content.media:description: The restaurant will be closed Friday after the building sustained extensive interior damage.

item.title: This is why regular eye exams matter as vision changes with age
item.dc:creator: LeAnne Gendreau, Katherine Ambrose , Sondra 'Sam' Cradduck , Amy Amy Cameron O’Rourke, Rhea Rogers
item.description: Our experts reveal why common age-related vision changes require regular medical exams rather than simple reading glasses.
item.content:encoded:
(Aging Untold) — Vision changes can be easy to brush off until everyday tasks — such as reading small print or seeing clearly at night — become more difficult.

Changes may be common with age, but eye exams can reveal more than vision problems and protecting your eyesight can help preserve independence.

Night vision changes and glare can be early warning signs

“Some of the symptoms that people will get will be like changes in the vision at nighttime,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.

Others experience difficulty with reading or glare.

“Or they have to adjust the distance from which they’re reading, either too close or too far. And there’s something that’s changing.” Rogers said.

Rogers said people may assume these changes are simply a normal part of getting older, but don’t dismiss vision changes as an inevitable part of aging. Some eye diseases can offer early signs of what is happening elsewhere in the body.

Eye exams can offer clues about overall health

Rogers said the eyes are among the body’s most energy-demanding organs.

Conditions such as diabetes and high blood pressure can increase oxidative stress, which Rogers described as damage to the mitochondria — the cells’ powerhouses.

Damage to mitochondria can contribute to deterioration in the eyes, Rogers said.

She recommends at least one regular eye exam once a year — at a minimum.

An exam might also reveal signs associated with diabetes, autoimmune diseases and blood pressure issues, gerontologist Sam Cradduck said. That means an exam is not only about checking whether someone needs a stronger prescription or reading glasses.

Amy shares a personal story

Aging expert Amy O’Rourke shared a personal story of how an eye exam prompted by difficulty with headlights led doctors to find a mole in the back of her eye that they are monitoring.

“I would encourage anybody to get regular eye exams because you just don’t know what’s going on,” O’Rourke host said.

The major eye conditions

Rogers said glaucoma, cataracts and macular degeneration are three major eye conditions to watch for.

Medicare coverage for vision care can be limited, but cataract treatment is covered, O’Rourke said.

Family history can also be important, especially for people whose relatives have had macular degeneration or glaucoma.

“If you’ve got a family history, your eye issues like macular degeneration and glaucoma, then you for sure ought to be very active in your eye care,” O’Rourke said.

The potential consequences of losing vision make eye care an important investment.

“You lose so much if you lose your vision,” O’Rourke said.

Protecting vision can help preserve independence

Vision affects more than the ability to read a label or drive at night. Ambrose said losing vision can affect a person’s ability to remain in their own home as well as everyday independence.

“This is really about independence,” Ambrose said. “Because when you lose vision, it can affect your ability to stay in your own home. It can affect just absolutely everything.”

Ambrose encouraged people to consider what steps they can take when changes begin.

5 key takeaways about aging and eye health

  1. Do not assume every change is normal aging. Some changes in vision may be connected to broader health concerns.
  2. Schedule regular eye exams. Dr. Rhea Rogers recommends exams at least once a year, while noting that people with conditions such as diabetes or high blood pressure may need particular attention to eye care.
  3. Know your family history. A family history of glaucoma or macular degeneration can make it especially important to be proactive about eye care.
  4. Think about independence. Protecting vision can help support everyday activities and the ability to remain in your own home.

item.title: New treatment could drastically reduce sepsis death rate, researcher says
item.dc:creator: Kristin Crowley
item.description: A doctor in Kansas City, Missouri, has made a discovery that could drastically reduce the amount of sepsis related deaths.
item.content:encoded:
(InvestigateTV) — Sepsis kills more than 350,000 adults and 1,800 children in the United States each year, according to the CDC. One in three adults who die in the hospital have sepsis.

A doctor in Kansas City, Missouri, has made a discovery that could drastically reduce that statistic.

What is sepsis?

Sepsis happens when the body’s immune system starts harming healthy tissues and organs in response to an infection, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

That can trigger a chain reaction throughout the body.

Early sepsis signs can start with a fever, chills and rapid breathing. Those symptoms then progress to confusion and difficulty breathing until it reaches the final stage, septic shock, which can lead to organ failure and death in as little as 12 hours, according to Sepsis Alliance.

A mother’s story

Two years ago, Brie Morgan Bauer was pregnant with her third child and excited to welcome him to a growing family. Everything about the pregnancy was normal until she felt flu-like symptoms at 27 weeks.

She went to her obstetrician’s office and that’s when the real emergency began.

“When they hooked me up, we were showing back-to-back contractions and I didn’t feel anything,” Bauer said. “But little did I know I was actually going septic.”

Bauer’s son, Bo, was delivered by emergency C-section. Her flu-like symptoms were strep throat. She went from bringing new life into the world to fighting for her own.

“By the third day that’s when they started looking at my toes, looking at my fingers and that they were turning purple and black,” Bauer said. “My hands were almost like mummified. They were black. And then I unwrapped my legs, and the legs were so crazy to see. The feet were definitely black.”

In her mind, Bauer thought there was no going back. “There’s no option to get blood flow back to a foot that is obviously dead.”

In the end, there was nothing she could have done to prevent what happened to her. She would have to live life as a quadruple amputee.

Brie's story | How her brother's kidney proved to be a perfect match

The current treatment for sepsis is antibiotics and IV fluids, which is sometimes not enough.

Researcher’s discovery

Dr. Cuthbert Simpkins has worked to find a solution to sepsis. He is the founder of Vivacell Bio Inc., where he has worked to find a solution to septic shock.

“There are 11 million cases around the world, and its mortality rate’s about 30%, 40%,” Simpkins said. “Depends on what stage you’re at, but if you’re at an advanced stage, it becomes almost 100%.”

Simpkins said during sepsis, the body makes too much nitric oxide, which leads to organ failure. His product, VBI-S, absorbs the nitric oxide, something Simpkins said has never been done before.

“It will act quickly, very quickly. You’ll see the blood pressure come up. You don’t have to wait to see its effect.”

He said that within 24 to 48 hours, “you’ll see the lungs get better, you’ll see the kidneys get better.”

In clinical trials, 80% of participants were expected to die from sepsis. VBI-S lowered that to 50%.

“They have shown that a high degree of efficacy in reversing failure of multiple organs,” Simpkins said.

He said the mortality rate would be even lower when the substance is given to patients early in their diagnosis. The clinical trials have concluded, and the product is awaiting FDA approval.

Other experts watching closely

Dr. Steven Simpson, a pulmonary and critical care doctor, is board chairman of the Sepsis Alliance, a group dedicated to finding a solution to sepsis.

“I am pleased that it seems to work as it’s intended to work,” Simpson said. “[It’s a] small study. We need a lot more patients treated. But very promising.”

Simpson said he sees patients in septic shock every day in the ICU.

He hopes, someday soon, no more will have to die from it. “It’s the reason that I work with Sepsis Alliance, it’s the reason for my entire career. It’s been 40 years, we haven’t found that solution yet.”

While Simpson doesn’t know if this will be a solution for sepsis, he is encouraged by the results.

“I don’t stick my neck out on what’s going to be the cure for sepsis. I am hopeful. I do believe that this is going to play a role, and I think it’s exciting,” he said.

Finding a new normal

Bauer was stunned to hear about the major discovery that could mean the end of sepsis.

I think that’s very promising," she said. “And I’m excited. I wish it was approved a while ago.”

VBI-S was not available for Bauer’s case. She has since found she has an interest in art and remains active in her sons’ lives.

“It’s been chaos. We live minute by minute,” Bauer said. “But my husband, he does everything. And I’m trying to do my best to find that more independence, more partnership with him to help reduce the chaos.”

“But that’s kind of what I’m showing my kids is what resilience looks like and to learn how to adapt,” Bauer said.

Bauer started a website, BriesHope.org, to offer support to survivors and families.

Simpkins said that with FDA approval, VBI-S could be in hospitals as soon as 2027.
